title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
hook: Pashupati, lord of every creature, and in Shaiva teaching the lord who loosens the rope

segments.voice: Yesterday the Shiva Sahasranama gave us its gentle names, Shankara and Shambhu, the fierce one who makes things well. What did that fierce person in your life protect? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.

Kathmandu, early morning, beside the Bagmati river. Monkeys run along the temple walls. Pigeons crowd the stone steps. Pilgrims queue with marigolds, and a little way down the bank, smoke rises from the cremation ghats. The temple is Pashupatinath, and the name over its door is one of Shiva's: Pashupati. The animals wandering the courtyard are a fitting welcome, because the name is about them, and then about all of us. It's today's selection from the Shiva Sahasranama, and the last stop of this week.
screen: `A TEMPLE ON THE BAGMATI.` → `MONKEYS, PIGEONS, PILGRIMS.` → `PASHUPATI.`

segments.voice: Pashupati joins two words. Pati is lord, or protector. Pashu is a creature, a beast, the kind of animal that's tied up in a yard: a cow, a goat. So at its simplest, Pashupati is the lord of animals, the herdsman god who looks after every living thing, wild and tame. The name sits in the sahasranama lists. But Shaiva teachers took it further. In schools such as Shaiva Siddhanta, three words carry the teaching. Pati, the lord, is Shiva. Pashu is every soul, you and me included, called a creature because it's tied. And pasha is the rope that ties it. Teachers name its strands: a root ignorance that makes the soul feel small, the pull of past actions, and the hold of the changing world. On this reading, Pashupati isn't only the lord who owns the herd. He's the one who loosens the rope. It's a humbling name and a hopeful one. Humbling, because it puts us in the yard with the goats. Hopeful, because a rope can be untied. Now look back over this week. We watched Nataraja, the dancer in the ring of fire, never still. Then the sahasranama called him Sthanu, the post that never moves. Then Shankara and Shambhu, the fierce one who makes things well. And today Pashupati, lord of every creature, the one who sets the tied one free. The names don't line up into one tidy picture. They keep turning him, the way you turn a stone in your hand to see every side.
screen: `PASHU, PATI: CREATURE, LORD.` · `PATI, PASHU, PASHA: LORD, SOUL, ROPE.` · `THE ONE WHO LOOSENS THE ROPE.` · `THIS WEEK: DANCER, POST, MAKER OF GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the rope, and give it some slack. Sit, and let the breath settle. Ask, quietly: what's pulling at me today? A worry, a habit, a grudge, a screen you keep reaching for. Don't fight it. Just feel where it tugs, in the chest, the belly, the hands. On each out-breath, let the rope go a little slack, the way you'd loosen a knot without cutting it. If you pray, you can say Pashupati and offer the knot to Shiva. If not, just let the breath loosen it. The bell holds the time.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Pashupati, lord of every creature, and in Shaiva teaching, the lord of the soul who loosens its rope.
Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Today, when you feel a familiar tug, name it as a rope, and see if you can give it one inch of slack. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-four.
